title: Optimizing Document Lookup: Making Atlas Search and Vector Search Up to 5x Faster
summary:
Sometimes the biggest performance gains come not from making core operations faster, but from eliminating unnecessary work surrounding them. That is exactly what we discovered while optimizing document lookup in MongoDB Atlas Search and Vector Search. By removing redundant query planning and execution overhead, we made search queries up to 5x faster without changing the underlying search algorithms.

When you run a $search or $vectorSearch query in MongoDB, two key stages work together to deliver the results. First, mongot, MongoDB's search process powered by Apache Lucene, executes the search query to identify and rank the most relevant documents. Then, mongod joins the search results with the corresponding BSON documents from the underlying collection using their _ids. The resulting documents can be further processed by additional aggregation pipeline stages before being returned to the application. Figure 1 illustrates this two-stage process:

Figure 1. Search execution in mongot and document materialization in mongod.

This second stage, known as document materialization, is handled by an internal aggregation stage called $_internalSearchIdLookup. While search execution has been extensively optimized, we discovered that document lookup had become a significant performance bottleneck. For every matching document, the stage repeatedly constructed a new query plan and acquired collection resources, introducing substantial overhead for queries returning hundreds or thousands of results. In our profiling, approximately 30% of mongod CPU time was spent on query planning and collection acquisition, rather than retrieving documents.

To address this, we redesigned the document lookup execution path to eliminate redundant query planning, reuse execution plans, and amortize resource acquisition across multiple lookups. The result: up to 4.9x faster $search queries, 5.5x faster $vectorSearch queries, and approximately 2.75x higher throughput under concurrency.

These optimizations shipped in MongoDB 9.0, are enabled by default, and require no application changes. In this post, we'll explore how we identified the bottleneck, redesigned the execution path, and achieved these performance improvements.

The hidden cost of repeated query planning

Looking up a document by its _id is typically a fast operation in MongoDB, thanks to its efficient _id index. However, the original $_internalSearchIdLookup implementation constructed and executed a new aggregation sub-pipeline for every document returned by mongot, even though only the _id value changed:

For each document, MongoDB parsed the query, optimized the pipeline, constructed an execution plan, acquired collection resources, attached a cursor, executed the lookup, and released resources.

The problem was not the indexed document retrieval, but the repeated preparation work surrounding it. Even though the query structure was identical across lookups, MongoDB rebuilt the execution plan and reacquired collection resources for every document instead of reusing them. This overhead accumulated linearly with the number of results. For example, a search query returning 1,000 documents could trigger 1,000 separate cycles of query planning, collection acquisition, and resource cleanup. As result sets grew, the repeated preparation work became a substantial contributor to end-to-end search latency. Figure 2 illustrates this repeated execution overhead.

Figure 2. Repeated query planning and resource acquisition for each document lookup.

To quantify this overhead, we profiled representative Vector Search workloads. The results revealed that approximately 30% of mongod CPU time was spent on query plan construction and collection acquisition, rather than retrieving documents. This confirmed that the bottleneck was not primarily the underlying document reads, but the redundant work surrounding them.

Redesigning the document lookup execution path

To eliminate redundant lookup overhead, we redesigned $_internalSearchIdLookup around two key optimizations: reusing parameterized execution plans and batching document lookups to minimize resource acquisition overhead. Together, these changes allow MongoDB to retrieve thousands of documents without repeatedly rebuilding query plans or acquiring collection resources.

1. Reusing a parameterized SBE execution plan

The first major optimization was introducing SbeSingleDocumentLookupExecutor, built on MongoDB's Slot-Based Execution (SBE) engine. The key observation was simple: every document lookup follows the same query structure, and only the _id value changes. Instead of constructing a new execution plan for each document, the optimized executor builds the lookup plan once, caches it, and reuses it by rebinding the _id parameter for subsequent lookups.

For example, when retrieving 1,000 documents, the original implementation could construct 1,000 separate query plans. With the optimized executor, all 1,000 lookups can reuse a single parameterized plan.

This eliminates redundant query parsing, optimization, and plan construction, significantly reducing per-document execution overhead.

2. Batching document lookups to reuse collection resources

While plan reuse eliminates repeated query planning, acquiring and releasing collection resources for every document can still introduce substantial overhead. To address this, we introduced a reusable BatchedEnrichmentStage that buffers incoming search results and processes them within a shared resource scope. Instead of independently acquiring and releasing collection resources for every document, the optimized execution path reuses collection resources across multiple lookups within a batch, amortizing the acquisition and cleanup costs. For example, with 1,000 documents and a batch size of 100, collection resources can be acquired just 10 times instead of 1,000 times, i.e., once per batch rather than once per document. Although the number of document lookups still grows linearly with the result set size, batching significantly reduces the repeated resource management overhead.

Combined with SBE plan caching, this allows thousands of document lookups to share both an execution plan and collection resources, substantially reducing CPU overhead. The result is a more efficient document lookup architecture: build the execution plan once, reuse it across documents, and minimize repeated resource acquisition.

Figure 3 illustrates how the optimized approach eliminates redundant work by reusing execution plans and collection resources across document lookups.

Figure 3. Original per-document lookup vs. optimized batched lookup with shared execution plans.

Performance results: End-to-end latency and throughput

As shown in Figure 4, both Atlas Search ($search) and Atlas Vector Search ($vectorSearch) achieved substantial reductions in end-to-end query latency across all evaluated result-set sizes (100, 1,000, and 10,000 documents). At 10,000 results, median latency dropped from approximately 2.6 seconds to 527 milliseconds for Atlas Search (4.9× faster) and from 3.1 seconds to 561 milliseconds for Atlas Vector Search (5.5× faster).

An important pattern emerges: the larger the result set, the greater the speedup. This is consistent with the underlying optimization. While search execution still incurs its own costs, eliminating repeated query planning and resource acquisition overhead becomes increasingly valuable as more documents are materialized.

Figure 4. End-to-end query latency improvements for Atlas Search and Atlas Vector Search in MongoDB 9.0.

Higher throughput under concurrency

Lower latency is only part of the story. We also evaluated performance under concurrent query execution. With 16 concurrent clients running a $search workload, the optimized implementation delivered:

  • Approximately 2.75x higher throughput

  • Approximately 3x lower median latency

These results demonstrate that the optimization does more than accelerate individual queries. By eliminating repeated query planning and resource acquisition, it reduces unnecessary CPU work per document lookup, allowing mongod to process more concurrent search requests with the same execution resources. The approximately 30% CPU overhead identified in our earlier profiling and the nearly 80% latency reduction observed in our benchmarks represent different measurements and workloads, rather than directly proportional improvements.

Real-world customer impact

To understand the potential impact on real-world workloads, we analyzed 163.8 million Atlas Vector Search executions across 610 customer clusters over 90 days. The analysis shows that larger result-set limits are used across a meaningful portion of the customer fleet. At least 40% of clusters execute queries with limits between 21 and 50, and at least 17% execute queries with limits above 100.

These workloads are particularly well-positioned to benefit from the document lookup optimizations, as eliminating repeated query planning and resource acquisition becomes increasingly valuable when more documents are retrieved.

Importantly, these improvements require no application changes. The optimized document lookup path is enabled by default in MongoDB 9.0.7. Applications do not need to rewrite queries, rebuild search indexes, or adopt new syntax. Existing $search and $vectorSearch pipelines can automatically benefit when running on supported configurations.

Faster search, without the extra work

This optimization began with a surprising observation: a simple _id lookup was spending a significant portion of its CPU budget preparing to execute rather than retrieving data. By replacing repeated aggregation planning with lightweight execution, introducing reusable batching infrastructure, and caching parameterized SBE plans, we removed a major source of overhead from Atlas Search and Vector Search. The result is up to 5.5× faster end-to-end queries in our benchmarks, along with substantial throughput improvements under concurrency.

More broadly, this work illustrates an important database engineering principle: sometimes the biggest performance gains come not from making the core operation faster, but from eliminating the unnecessary work surrounding it. This effort was made possible through collaboration across MongoDB’s Atlas Search Query, Query Execution, Query Integration, Database Integration and Observability, and Server Triage & Release teams. Special thanks to Denis Grebennicov from the Database Integration and Observability team for his significant contributions to this optimization effort.

title: The $5 Trillion Shift: Preparing Retail Backends for the Age of AI Agents
summary:
Retail is entering the era of the multi-agent shopping assistant. Instead of a single, stateless chatbot following a rigid script, retailers are building systems where multiple agents collaborate behind the scenes, drawing on preferences and customer purchase history to deliver recommendations that improve with every interaction. More retailers are reconfiguring their backends to reflect the rise in agentic usage, as this is no small trend: McKinsey estimates AI agents could mediate $3 trillion to $5 trillion of global consumer commerce by 2030.(1)

The need is real, as the race is heating up to quickly respond to customer searches and take service to another level. A customer searching for a pair of running shoes for an upcoming marathon no longer triggers a keyword search. The query kicks off a coordinated reasoning process across multiple specialized agents. This has to happen rapidly and seamlessly to keep consumers' attention and needs met.

The promise of this shift is real, but the real architectural question has nothing to do with which LLM or orchestration framework a team chooses. It has everything to do with where the data lives and whether every agent can see the same version of the truth simultaneously. Increasingly, retailers are finding that solution in MongoDB.

The technology challenge behind multi-agent AI

Building a single AI agent is straightforward with modern LLMs and orchestration frameworks. Building a production multi-agent system is not. Why? Agentic AI has five distinct data needs:

  • Semantic search over vector embeddings 

  • Flexible user context 

  • Conversation state across sessions 

  • Long-term memory that evolves over time 

  • Observability through audit logs

Engineering teams pay a heavy ‘siloed database tax’ to meet these needs, standing up five distinct, single-purpose datastores: a vector store for product discovery, a session store for chat history, a short-term memory store for session context, a long-term memory store for accumulated preferences, and an audit log for compliance and debugging.

That fragmentation comes at a cost. Every additional datastore adds its own SDK, its own operational overhead, and its own failure mode. If the profile agent writes a new preference to one store while the product agent reads from another, the two are only as consistent as the ETL job connecting them. In a real-time conversation, that gap shows up as an agent recommending a product the customer already ruled out, or forgetting a preference captured moments earlier.

Retail makes the problem concrete. Carol asks for running shoes for a road marathon. Her profile has her static preference on file: She wears a size eight. Earlier in this conversation, she mentioned wanting maximum cushioning; that's short-term session context. John asks for running shoes, too. His profile puts him at a size 11, but long-term memory holds something neither his profile nor this conversation does: He needs a waterproof build, a fact learned from a past return after a pair let water soak in. Serving both well, consistently, and across every channel requires holding all three—static preferences, session context, and long-term memory—as one coherent view. This is what we’ve built to make this all happen fluidly

Giving every agent the same context

Retailers building a multi-agent system need specialized agents—including planner agents, profile agents, product agents, and eventually others—to discover and invoke each other's capabilities regardless of which team built them. This is what an open protocol like Agent2Agent (A2A) (2) provides. The Multi Agent Retail Advisor (MARA) is a reference implementation. Here, a planner agent delegates to a profile agent and a product agent, coordinating through A2A. The orchestration framework and LLM are both swappable; MongoDB, the data layer underneath every agent, is not.

Figure 1. Reference architecture for the MARA, showing how the planner, profile, and product agents interact through the A2A protocol, with MongoDB Atlas unifying operational and agentic data via Vector Search, text search, and auto-embeddings.

MongoDB Atlas handles all five agentic data needs natively in one platform, as shown in Figure 2 below. Atlas Vector Search stores product embeddings alongside the catalog data itself, so semantic search runs directly against operational data instead of a separate index to remain in sync. The same flexible document model holds customer context and preferences without a schema migration every time a field changes. Short-term memory lives as a nested array inside each session document, allowing the planner agent to fetch an entire conversation in one read. Long-term memory accumulates in its own collection, capturing facts an agent learns about a customer, like a preference for polyester base layers because they dry faster, independent of any single session. Observability runs through the same platform, too, logging every tool call's inputs, outputs, and latency so a request's full execution path can be reconstructed instantly.

Figure 2. MongoDB Atlas consolidates all single-purpose datastores to meet agentic AI’s data needs into one platform.

For product discovery, retailers build directly on Atlas Vector Search. They embed queries with Voyage AI and match them semantically against the catalog, falling back automatically to Atlas full-text search on the same collection when a query needs it, with no extra infrastructure. Because Voyage AI's newer models share a common embedding space, retailers can embed the catalog once with a larger, accurate model, and then run live queries with a smaller, faster model without ever re-indexing.

A simpler, more resilient stack for IT teams

For retailers, the payoff is architectural simplicity that compounds into speed and cost savings. Teams no longer manage four or five separate systems; they manage one. Schema flexibility, shown in Figure 3, lets agent state and user profiles, each varying by shopper or task, evolve without disruptive migrations. Because MongoDB Atlas scales horizontally, it supports the bursty, unpredictable request patterns of autonomous agents without becoming a bottleneck. Full observability works the same way: A single aggregation pipeline query joins the tool_invocations log, agent_state history, and session record for a request, reconstructing what each agent did, in what order, and how long each step took. That gives IT teams a queryable execution trace for every agent decision, shortening the path from a production issue to a root cause.

Figure 3. Two documents from the agent_state collection and two from the users collection. This shows the same collection, different shape, depending on which agent ran or which shopper it describes.

This consolidation also changes how fast a team can move. The product catalog, user profiles, session history, long-term memory, and tool-invocation logs all live as collections in one MongoDB cluster, not four separate systems linked together. That's the difference between a proof of concept shipping in weeks and one spending its first quarter wiring systems together before a single agent runs.  This setup lowers total cost of ownership the same way: one licensing agreement, one scaling model, and one team. Governance benefits too. Fine-grained access controls, encryption, and audit logging apply consistently across every agent's data, instead of system-by-system configuration. Because the architecture is not tied to a specific framework or model provider, retailers can add new agents, inventory, loyalty, and fulfillment onto the same data plane without replatforming. That matters most for agents no one can name yet. Any future agent built on the same document model plugs into the same unified context, turning what would otherwise be a multi-quarter integration effort into a schema extension.

An experience that feels seamless for customers

For customers, this translates into an experience that feels genuinely continuous. Because every agent reads from and writes to the same unified context, a preference shared in one conversation carries into the next. A question that starts in a chat can hand off cleanly to an inventory agent checking store stock or a loyalty agent applying a reward without the customer repeating themselves. This results in recommendations that get sharper the more a customer interacts with the system and a shopping experience that feels like one relationship rather than a series of disconnected sessions.

Figure 4. Any multi-agent retail architecture needs a swappable layer for orchestration and the LLM, but every agent still needs one constant data layer underneath it. Here, that's MongoDB Atlas beneath MARA's planner, profile, and product agents.

That continuity holds up across channels, not just across conversation turns. A preference a customer states while browsing on mobile is available the next time they open a chat window, walk into a store, or call support because it lives in the same unified profile every agent reads from rather than in a channel-specific cache. Customers also benefit from recommendations that account for their actual history rather than generic popularity signals. This happens since the product agent's semantic search runs against a catalog informed by what a shopper has already bought, browsed, and rejected. For the business, that precision compounds directly into commerce metrics: higher conversion, larger basket sizes, and fewer costly returns from recommendations that miss the mark.

Building for what comes next

The orchestration framework and LLM a retailer chooses today will likely change more than once. What shouldn't change is the data layer holding the system together. MongoDB gives retailers a single, flexible foundation for the knowledge, context, memory, and observability multi-agent retail experiences depend on, so the architecture underneath doesn't have to be rebuilt as frameworks and models evolve. Retailers that consolidate this layer now will be the ones ready to add the next agent—and the next protocol—without starting over.

References

  1. The automation curve in agentic commerce. McKinsey. January 28th, 2026. https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/quantumblack/our-insights/the-automation-curve-in-agentic-commerce

  2. Getting Started with Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol https://codelabs.developers.google.com/intro-a2a-purchasing-concierge#0

title: How to Model an Insurance Policy Without Joining Dozens of Tables
summary:
Ask an underwriter to describe a policy, and you’ll get a coherent answer: A contract, for a customer, covering a car or a house, with a handful of coverages, each with a limit and a deductible, plus a history of every change since it was issued. One policy—with parts. Many parts.

Now ask your database the same question. In most insurance core systems, that single policy is sliced across dozens of relational tables: one each for coverages, vehicles, named parties, endorsements, and billing schedules. Every time a screen loads, the system reassembles the policy by joining those tables back together. Every time a product changes, several of the tables need altering. When Manulife rebuilt its policy servicing platform, its chief architect described replacing more than 500 core tables with one document per policy and reported that the new system won overwhelming approval from its developers.

That gap—between how the business thinks about a policy and how the database stores it—is the central problem a document database like MongoDB solves. This blog post explains the one design decision that matters most when you make that move and why it’s an insurance decision as much as a technical one.

One rule drives everything

A document database stores records as nested structures, closer to a folder than a spreadsheet row. A policy document can hold its coverages, its vehicles, its parties, and its event history all within itself. The temptation is to simply pour the old table diagram into this new shape. That’s the wrong instinct.

The core idea is to model the data around what the business does with it, not around how the entities look on a diagram. Concretely, that means designing for the policy lifecycle (quote, underwrite, issue, bill, endorse, renew, cancel, claim) and asking, at each step, what gets read and written together.

Once you ask that question, every design choice reduces to one decision: whether to embed or reference.

Embed or reference: The decision that matters

For any two related pieces of data, you have two options. Embed one inside the other, so they live in a single document. Or reference one from the other, storing just an identifier that points to a separate document, the way a relational foreign key does.

The test can be reduced to two very simple statements:

  • Embed data that is part of something and is always read alongside it.

  • Reference data that has its own lifecycle or is shared across many records.

Apply that to a policy and the answers fall out naturally. Coverages belong inside the policy. Nobody ever looks up collision coverage without the policy it sits within. The insured vehicle belongs inside the policy—as does the event history, because an endorsement or a cancellation is meaningless apart from the contract it changed. In document form, that looks like this:

Anyone in the business can read that. It looks like the policy.

The claim follows the same logic, with a payoff that finance teams will appreciate. A claim’s reserves and payments belong inside the claim document. Because a single document is always written atomically, posting a reserve and updating the claim’s total becomes one operation that either fully succeeds or doesn’t happen at all. There’s no window where the ledger and the claim disagree.

Now let’s look at the other side of the test. A customer’s policies should not be embedded inside the customer record. Policies are large, they change constantly, and they’re almost always looked up by policy number rather than through the customer record. Instead, store policies in their own collection and have each policy reference its customer by ID. Claims should not be embedded inside policies either, because a claim can outlive the policy that spawned it: a canceled policy can still have open claims. Store claims separately, with each claim referencing the policy it belongs to.

The agent who sold the policy and the product it was written on should also be referenced, not embedded, and here the reasoning is operational. Thousands of policies share one agent and one product. Embed the agent’s details, and a change to their license number becomes a write across every policy in their book. Keep the product catalog as the single, versioned source of truth, and let the policy store only a point-in-time snapshot of the coverage terms it was bound against.

Two storms that test the design

Insurance also stress-tests data models in a way few other industries do: catastrophes.

The hurricane claim

Most auto and property claims carry fewer than 10 supporting attachments (photos, estimates, or a police report, for example). Embedding them in the claim is fine. But a major-loss claim after a hurricane can accumulate 60 or more attachments. MongoDB has a hard 16 MB size limit per document, but even well below that, a bloated minority of claims slows down every screen that loads them.

The wrong fix is to move all claim documents into a separate collection “just in case,” penalizing the 99% for the 1%. The right fix is what MongoDB’s engineers call the outlier pattern: embed by default, and when a claim crosses a threshold, flip an overflow flag and store the excess in a side collection. The design serves the common case and handles the exception explicitly.

Here’s what that looks like for a hurricane claim. Once the claim crosses the threshold, the application sets the flag and moves the extra documents to the side collection, so the claim record stays small:

The wildfire intake surge

When a database outgrows one server, MongoDB splits it across several, and a field called the shard key decides which server each record lands on. It seems sensible to shard claims by catastrophe (CAT) event code, since the CAT dashboard queries by it. It’s a trap. During an active wildfire, nearly every new claim for days shares one CAT code, so every new claim routes to one server—precisely when intake throughput matters most. Use a hashed shard key on the claim number to spread new claims evenly, and keep the CAT code as an ordinary index for the dashboard.

Both examples carry the same lesson: The data model is where operational resilience is decided, long before the storm arrives.

Three patterns to adopt on day one

Beyond the embed-versus-reference rule, there are three more design patterns to adopt:

  1. Computed totals. Store “total incurred” and “total paid” on the claim rather than re-summing reserves and payments on every read. Claim detail is among the busiest screens in the company; don’t make it do math.

  2. Schema versioning. Stamp every policy and claim with a version number. Insurance records survive for decades under regulatory retention and litigation discovery, and your document shape will change over that time. Without a version marker, that drift becomes an audit problem, not just a technical one. Travelers Insurance is reported to have eliminated a three-day wait for schema changes after moving off a rigid relational model; versioning is what makes that agility safe.

  3. Append-only history. Policy events, claim activity, and increasingly, the step-by-step decision trace of any automated underwriting or fraud-screening agent should only ever be added to, never edited or deleted. In most industries, that’s good hygiene. In insurance, it’s compliance. As regulators turn their attention to AI-driven decisions, an auditable trace of what an automated system decided and why will be the difference between a quick review and a drawn-out one.

What this means for you

None of this requires your engineers to abandon what they know. Multi-document transactions still exist for the moments that need them, such as binding a submission into a policy. The shift is in the starting question. Instead of “What are the entities and how do they relate?” it becomes, “What does the business read and write together, and what changes on its own?”

Keep what’s always read together, well, together. Separate what lives its own life. Plan explicitly for the outlier and the surge. Get those right, and the database finally describes a policy the way your underwriters do.

title: How Observe.AI Used MongoDB Resharding to Scale Its AI Platform
summary:
Launched in 2017, Observe.AI was originally known for its expertise in conversation intelligence and contact center analytics. In recent years, however, the company has grown into a comprehensive agentic AI platform, and now has three core offerings:

  • AI agents for customers that resolve customer requests across voice and chat.

  • AI agents for frontline teams. These include Observe.AI’s recently launched Companion Agent, which provides human team members real-time guidance and automates work before, during, and after customer interactions.

  • AI agents for operations that evaluate interactions, generate coaching, uncover operational insights, and drive continuous improvement across contact centers.

Observe.AI uses MongoDB Atlas as the foundational data layer for its AI platform and relies on it to store raw customer conversations, AI-generated enrichments, model configurations, and agent metadata.

MongoDB's flexible document model enables rapid iteration as AI models evolve, while its scalability—supporting over 100 clusters and 50+ TB of data—has made it the trusted system of record powering our platform's intelligence layer.

Recently, the team wanted to continue scaling with MongoDB in a way that preserved application availability, reduced operational risk, and created a predictable runway for continued data growth.

The team partnered with MongoDB Consulting’s professional services to scale a production-critical MongoDB Atlas deployment to support Observe.AI’s conversation intelligence platform. The project was a joint engineering effort between Observe.AI and MongoDB that used MongoDB resharding as a practical, online mechanism for redistributing large collections across a broader shard footprint.

Expanding a constrained shard footprint

At the time of the project, the cluster had the following characteristics:

  • A sharded MongoDB Atlas deployment with two data shards plus config servers.

  • Approximately 13 TB of compressed data per data shard, representing roughly 50 TB of uncompressed data overall.

  • Each shard runs on the M140 tier with a disk limit of approximately 14 TB, leaving limited available headroom.

  • A sustained ingest rate of roughly 50 GB per day, making proactive capacity expansion important for safe long-term operations.

  • Several multi-TB collections with significant index footprint and production traffic. This setup had worked at an early stage in the company's cycle, but was no longer fit for purpose and could lead to performance issues or service degradation that would directly impact customers.

The engineering objective of the MongoDB–Observe.AI effort was clear: to expand a constrained shard footprint to a healthier horizontal layout, while also keeping the application online and minimizing disruption to production workloads.

Beyond balancer: a faster redistribution for large-scale data movements

After adding new shard capacity, the team evaluated the default balancer-driven redistribution path. They determined that the balancer was the right tool for ongoing incremental balancing, but the volume of data to be redistributed was large enough that relying on chunk migrations alone would have extended the migration window and kept the original shards under elevated pressure for longer than desired.

The team also tackled a number of other constraints. First, the new shard capacity could receive data, but the pace of redistribution was bounded by balancer and range-deletion throughput; range deletion also created additional background load on shards that were already carrying production traffic. Secondly, existing shards periodically experienced high WiredTiger cache pressure, making it important to avoid prolonged competition between application traffic, balancing, and cleanup activity. Finally, the team wanted a controlled, predictable migration path rather than an extended background redistribution process.

They concluded that the balancer should continue to handle incremental corrections, but a faster and more explicit redistribution mechanism was needed for the initial large-scale data movement.

The four-step resharding plan

Instead of relying solely on balancer migrations, the MongoDB–Observe.AI team designed a controlled resharding plan:

  1. Scale out the cluster

    • Increase capacity by adding multiple new shards (not just one) so that, after redistribution, each shard would hold a manageable share of the ~50 TB dataset.

  2. Prepare the cluster for resharding

    • Ensure no ongoing migrations or resharding jobs.

    • Pin the config servers to remain embedded/dedicated as appropriate for this topology.

    • Disable range deletions and disallow chunk migrations for critical collections so that resharding traffic does not compete with the balancer and range deleter for IOPS.

  3. Run resharding on the largest collections

    • For each large collection (collection6, collection7, collection8, etc.), run reshardCollection to redistribute data across the new shard set, keeping the same shard key but changing the ownership distribution.

    • Execute resharding sequentially per collection to avoid overloading donors, recipients, or the config server.

Table 1. Resharding performance metrics.

4. Clean up and return to normal operations

  • Once data has been redistributed:
    • Remove old empty shards from the cluster.
    • Remove temporary zone configurations that were only needed during the migration.
    • Re‑enable balancing and range deletions for the now‑healthy collections.

Resharding driving greater optimization, performance, and reliability

The joint effort gave Observe.AI a safer and more scalable data foundation for continued platform growth.

Thanks to resharding, the cluster moved from a limited disk runway to a healthier multi-month capacity position, while large multi-TB collections were redistributed across the expanded shard footprint using online resharding rather than relying only on extended balancer-driven chunk migration.

Production reads and writes continued during the clone and catch-up phases, with only the final commit phase requiring a brief write-blocking critical section. The team reduced sustained pressure on the original shards and created more room for future ingest growth, maintenance, and operational flexibility.

Finally, after the migration, the MongoDB balancer returned to its normal role of incremental rebalancing, while the heavy data movement was handled through the more appropriate resharding workflow.

The project highlighted how sharding and resharding can be used proactively as part of ongoing capacity management, helping optimize storage utilization, manage growing data volumes, and maintain platform performance and reliability as workloads scale.

Combining horizontal scale-out and resharding: A winning combo

The key idea behind MongoDB’s resharding capability is simple—sharding should not be the last‑resort, once‑in‑a‑lifetime operation you dread. It should be a practical, fast tool you can use whenever your workload outgrows its current shape.

If you treat sharding as “too expensive” and delay it until your primary is holding tens of TBs, you pay that cost back many times in:

  • Oversized single replica sets,

  • Operational risk,

  • And slow, painful balancing when you finally add shards.

By combining horizontal scale-out with resharding, which has been available since MongoDB 8.0 launched in 2024, you can start small, grow organically, and still have a predictable, efficient path to redistribute data when your cluster—and your business—takes off.

Observe.AI’s  platform processes billions of customer interactions each year, so the infrastructure has to scale as seamlessly as the business. Working alongside the MongoDB team enabled Observe.AI to redistribute more than 50 TB of production data with virtually no disruption to customers. MongoDB 8.0 resharding provided  the operational confidence to expand capacity proactively instead of reacting to infrastructure limits, allowing Observe.AI’s engineering teams to stay focused on delivering innovation for customers.

title: Introducing the MongoDB Vercel AI SDK Integration: Persistent Memory for AI Applications
summary:
We are excited to announce the release of the MongoDB Vercel AI SDK integration, which provides AI applications and agents built with Vercel’s SDK with a persistent memory store in MongoDB Atlas. It's now open source and generally available on npm.

This integration adds MongoDB Atlas as the memory store in the existing Vercel AI SDK code. Once installed, the package connects Vercel AI SDK applications to MongoDB Atlas and automatically stores the application's memories in documents. This allows the application to retain memories about conversations, user facts, and past events that persist across sessions, users, and restarts.

What is the Vercel AI SDK?

The Vercel AI SDK is a TypeScript toolkit for building AI applications. It handles calling models, streaming responses, using tools, and running agents that work through multi-step tasks. The SDK doesn't include a database to persist memories between runs. Without memory, an AI application starts every conversation with no knowledge of the last one. It doesn't know who the user is, what they asked yesterday, or what it learned along the way. It doesn’t have any context.

Today, developers have to build their own tooling to store memories in a layer. That usually means designing a database schema, writing jobs to clear out old data, and setting up vector search so the application can find relevant past information by semantic meaning instead of just keywords. It's a lot of work to build an AI application that can remember context.

What types of memory does an AI application need?

An AI application needs five kinds of memory, each kept for a different length of time and retrieved differently. This integration automatically categorizes each type of memory and stores it in MongoDB Atlas; here are short definitions of the five memory types:

  • Session: The conversation an application or agent has in each session. This helps the application follow what the user just said.

title: Introducing the MongoDB Claude SDK Session Adapter: Durable Session Storage for Agents
summary:
The Claude Agent SDK is a package that lets you embed Claude Code's own agent loop directly into your application: web search, file search, file editing, MCP server connections, and more, all without having to define those tools or manage the agent loop yourself. The SDK also automatically persists session transcripts to the local file system by default. Claude calls it the Agent SessionStore.

Today, we are excited to announce the MongoDB Claude SDK Session Adapter, available in Python (with TypeScript coming in January 2027).

What is the Claude Agent SessionStore?

But first, let's understand what a SessionStore actually is. It is the extension point in the Claude Agent SDK for saving an agent's session outside the machine where it ran. Configure one, and the SDK mirrors every conversation turn and action as the agent works, so the session can pick back up exactly where it left off, on any instance that has access to that store.

That matters most once an agent stops running on a single, persistent machine. Say a team deploys their Claude agent as a Lambda function, callable as an internal service by teams across the company. Every invocation is a disposable instance; there's no local disk to store anything between calls. Without a SessionStore, each request is stateless by default; the agent has no memory of what came before. With a configured SessionStore, any invocation can pick up a session's full history, regardless of which instance handled the last turn.

That is the gap the MongoDB Session Adapter closes.

This is especially useful for enterprises that have multiple teams developing agents across many machines, who need session storage that survives host failures, scales as the agent fleet increases, and enforces the same access controls and retention rules as the rest of their data estate, not a bolt-on system built solely for agent memory.

The MongoDB Claude SDK Session Adapter

The MongoDB Claude SDK Session Adapter gives Claude agents durable session storage: a record of the conversation and its action history that lets an agent pick back up exactly where it left off, whether that's on the same laptop, a different server, or any server in a distributed deployment.

The adapter helps cover three crucial areas:

  • Cross-environment continuity: Whether a different backend instance picks up a conversation after a restart or a user resumes on a different device, session state doesn't live on the machine that started it. Because every step is mirrored to MongoDB as it happens, any instance in your deployment can resume exactly where the last one left off.

  • Resilience to failure: If a host crashes or a container gets rescheduled mid-conversation, nothing is lost. Entries are written to MongoDB as they occur, not batched or cached locally, so whichever instance picks the session back up sees the same state as the failed one, up to the last completed step.

  • Retention and auditability: Many teams need to retain agent transcripts to meet internal data-retention or audit requirements. Instead of standing up a separate system just for that, session data lives in the MongoDB cluster you're already operating, under the same access controls and backup policies as the rest of your data.

title: Introducing the MongoDB Google ADK Integration: Durable Memory for Agent State
summary:
We’re excited to announce the MongoDB Google ADK Integration, which provides developers with the building blocks they need to create durable memory for agent state.

As agents move from prototypes to real-world applications, they need secure, dependable access to data and the ability to retain context over a long time. However, developers still need to build their own tooling for a data store that provides durable agent memory for agent state. 

This integration gives developers a cohesive, ADK-native experience for using MongoDB as the data platform for agents.

What is the Google ADK?

The Google Agent Development Kit (ADK) is an open source agent development framework that lets you build, debug, and deploy reliable AI agents at enterprise scale. It is available in Python, TypeScript, Go, Java, and Kotlin.

Google ADK offers developers an extensive set of tools for creating, deploying, assessing, and scaling agents, enabling developers to build anything from personal AI assistants to mission-critical business workflows.

How does the MongoDB Google ADK Integration help?

Developers can prototype an agent that searches a product catalog or knowledge base, then evolve it into a production experience that preserves user context across conversations and recalls relevant prior interactions. With MongoDB as the data layer, developers can keep the data their agents search over, the conversation state that needs to survive a restart or a scaled-out instance, and the memories agents build over time, all in the same place as the rest of their application data. That means no separate database to stand up for retrieval, no pipeline syncing app data into a different memory index, and no added latency pulling context from another system before the agent can respond.

ADK supplies the agent framework and tool interface; this integration provides the data and persistence layer beneath it, so developers can easily take an agent from prototype to production. These agents can maintain conversation and session memory independent of any single machine, and carry a user's history across sessions.

Providing a unified agent architecture

At the core of this integration is Google ADK 2.0, which serves as the code-first orchestration layer for multi-agent systems. ADK 2.0 provides the deployment framework, while MongoDB provides session and memory storage for agents.

Integrating directly with the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, ADK 2.0 eliminates the need for custom routing logic by providing standardized tool-calling interfaces, native telemetry, and enterprise access controls out of the box. Developers can use Gemini 4 Argon for multi-step reasoning and Gemini 3.8 Flash for low-latency execution.

Figure 1. The MongoDB Google ADK Integration adds session and memory storage for single or multi-agent workflows.

How do Sessions and Memory storage work?

Great agent experiences improve with context. This integration introduces MongoDbSessionService to persist sessions, events, and application-, user-, and session-scoped state to MongoDB.

This means developers can build agents that retain the context needed for longer-running and multi-turn interactions. The session service includes optimistic concurrency control to help applications safely manage concurrent updates, while configurable collections make it easier to fit the service into existing data architectures.

For agents that need memory beyond a single session, MongoDBMemoryService ingests session events into MongoDB collections and recalls relevant memories through keyword matching. Memory ingestion is idempotent, which prevents duplicates when a session is added again.

Together, these services help agents become more useful over time without requiring developers to stitch together separate systems for retrieval, state, and memory.

How does MongoDB Search help agents with data retrieval?

Having memory for agent state is essential, but agents also need fast access to the operational data they search over, the same product catalogs, documents, and records your application already queries. This is where MongoDB's built-in search capabilities come in. MongoDB Vector Search leverages Voyage AI's embedding models, which are the same engine backing MemoryService's semantic retrieval in this integration.

Developers can also perform hybrid search by combining vector search with full-text search using the $rankFusion aggregation stage.

This gives agents access to the right information and context at the right time, delivering better responses in production. Whether you are building product discovery, knowledge assistants, support experiences, or domain-specific copilots, agents can automatically leverage semantic and hybrid retrieval to ground their responses in your data.

The application owns the database connection, database name, and search configuration. The agent gets focused tools to call, without exposing those operational details in its context.

Using MongoDB as the operational data store, the memory layer for agent state, and the search engine over both, developers get one platform instead of three, on whatever deployment they run it on. There's no separate vector database to stand up, no search engine to sync against a second copy of the data, and no added latency from hopping between systems before the agent can respond.

Which deployment versions does this integration support?

The integration supports MongoDB Atlas and self-managed MongoDB 8.0+ deployments for vector and hybrid search. Developers can provide a connection string or bring an existing PyMongo client, and configure search behavior through MongoDbToolSettings, including index names, embedding fields, limits, and candidate counts.

That flexibility makes it possible to align the integration with existing data models, deployment choices, and performance requirements.

title: Atlas Data Federation and Online Archive Can Now Be Deployed in Azure
summary:
Exciting developments are on the horizon for users of Microsoft Azure, marking a significant leap in data management capabilities. First off, Atlas Data Federation is now Generally Available on Azure. Atlas Data Federation is now generally available for deployment in Azure. An Azure deployment can query data in Microsoft Azure Blob Storage, alongside other supported sources. And that's not all. We've also launched the General Availability of Atlas Online Archive on Azure. These advancements usher in a new era of efficient archiving solutions for Azure-based data solutions.

Both updates are big steps forward in making data management on Azure more powerful and flexible. Let's dive into what this means for you!

Azure support in Atlas Data Federation (General Availability)

Atlas Data Federation can query across multiple supported sources, including Atlas clusters and cloud object storage. It supports S3 or Azure Blob Storage as a source, but does not support querying S3 and Azure Blob Storage together in the same federated database instance/query. This feature, previously exclusive to AWS, is a game-changer, allowing direct deployment within Azure and the ability to tap into Microsoft Azure Blob Storage for data insights.

Key features of Atlas Data Federation

  • Cloud flexibility: Deployment choice: Deploy Atlas Data Federation in AWS or Azure. Cloud storage sources are queried within the supported provider configuration; cross-cloud queries between AWS S3 and Azure Blob Storage are not supported.
  • Diverse data sources: For Azure deployments, query Atlas cluster data with supported Azure storage sources, including Azure Blob Storage and Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2. Atlas Data Federation does not combine Azure storage and AWS S3 in the same federated query.
  • Advanced aggregation: Comprehensive aggregation capabilities with operators inclusive of $match, $lookup, $queryHistory, $merge, $out, etc.
    • Direct $out support for Azure Blob Storage and Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2.
  • Atlas SQL queries on Azure: Execute SQL queries on Azure, integrating MongoDB data for a unified analysis experience.

Atlas Data Federation simplifies accessing and analyzing complex data sets by combining data across multiple sources into a single, federated view, providing valuable insights for more informed business decisions.

A federated configuration supports at most one configured instance each of AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage, and Google Cloud Storage. This does not enable querying across cloud providers; S3 and Azure Blob Storage cannot be queried together in one federated database instance/query.

Explore Atlas Data Federation on Azure Today.

Azure support in Atlas Online Archive (General Availability)

Atlas Online Archive's expansion to Azure ensures that data tiering is not only efficient but also integrated, keeping archival data within the Azure ecosystem. This integration addresses the previous limitation of defaulting to AWS for storage, even for Azure-hosted clusters.

Key features of Atlas Online Archive

  • Provider choice: Opt for AWS or Azure to align with your cloud strategy.
  • Automatic archiving: Set rules to move older data to cost-effective cloud storage automatically, eliminating manual offloading.
  • Unified querying endpoint: Access all data through a single endpoint, ensuring quick insights without compromising data availability.
  • Integrated MongoDB Atlas UI management: Manage your data tiering and archiving within the familiar Atlas interface, streamlining operations and maintenance.

Seamlessly manage your MongoDB Atlas data tiering at scale with Atlas Online Archive. Atlas Online Archive empowers you to manage your data lifecycle efficiently, balancing cost and accessibility with ease.

Finally, here are a few points to consider:

  • Any newly created archive on an Azure cluster on or after 02/28 will default to Azure regions. Note that storage regions for Online Archive will default to Azure clusters only if there are no pre-existing AWS archives on that specific Azure cluster
  • If there are any pre-existing AWS Online Archives on Azure clusters, then all newly created archives on that specific cluster will remain on AWS.
  • Cloud providers or storage regions cannot be edited or modified once configured

Embrace the Full Potential of Atlas Online Archive on Azure Today.

We're thrilled to support your data management journey, offering enhanced control and flexibility over your data through these new Azure capabilities. As MongoDB Atlas continues to expand as a multi-cloud solution, we're here to ensure your data strategy is as dynamic and versatile as your business needs.

For guidance on getting started, check out our documentation on Atlas Data Federation or Atlas Online Archive.

Thank you for trusting MongoDB Atlas as your modern database. Welcome to expanded cloud deployment and storage options for Atlas Data Federation and Online Archive.

title: AI Search for Agents: Announcing Automated Embedding in MongoDB Atlas
summary:
Automated Embedding is now available in Public Preview on MongoDB Atlas.

When we introduced Automated Embedding to MongoDB Vector Search in MongoDB Community Edition, we started from a single principle: developers building agentic applications shouldn't have to operate a parallel embedding pipeline just to search their own data. That release proved the pattern: text in, text out, no client-side embedding code. On MongoDB Atlas, it goes further, using Voyage AI embedding models to solve the operational problems that have made vector search the most fragile part of an agent stack.

Figure 1. Automated Embedding flow in MongoDB Atlas.

Your vector search index falls behind your data

A document gets edited. The vector store still has the old embedding. The agent retrieves stale context and confidently answers based on outdated information. The fix has historically been a backfill job, written by a human, scheduled by a human, and debugged by a human. The time between "data changed" and "index reflects it" is measured in hours, not seconds.

Automated Embedding solves this with field-level delta detection. When a document changes, MongoDB Atlas re-embeds only when an indexed field actually changes. Sync is near real-time, not batch. There is no manual re-index path because there's no manual index to maintain. For agents, this is the difference between trustworthy memory and stale context.

The same property extends to search on views. If your embedding source is a $concat of title, cast, and year, an update to any of those underlying fields automatically propagates through the view to the index.

One inference pool can't serve every workload

Embedding inference is the throughput problem hiding inside a latency problem. A first-time backfill needs to chew through tens of millions of documents as fast as possible. A live query needs a vector back in tens of milliseconds. A change stream sits in between, bursty, sometimes idle, and sometimes hot. One inference pool serves all three workloads poorly: tune it for throughput and queries time out; tune it for latency, and backfills take a week.

Automated Embedding separates inference into two mechanisms, each optimized for the workload it serves:

  • Index builds are throughput-optimized using a newly introduced Inference Flex Tier, enabling them to go from zero to fully indexed without competing with live queries. Variable but unbounded throughout.
  • Queries are latency-optimized, completing within the time budget agents actually have. Guaranteed but bounded throughput.

A backfill no longer slows your queries, and your queries no longer cap your backfill rate.

At scale, storage and indexing both break

Float32 vectors are honest but expensive. A million 1024-dimensional embeddings is roughly 4 GB before you've stored a single byte of operational data. At a hundred million vectors, storage cost becomes the line item, retrieval latency suffers, and the team starts asking whether they really need 1024 dimensions or whether 512 would do. That's a guess most teams shouldn't be making.

Storage isn't the only thing that breaks at scale.

One document per inference request wastes orders of magnitude of throughput. Hand-tuned batching helps until you hit a document shape that exceeds the model's token window mid-batch, at which point the whole request fails. Errors at this scale don't fail one document; they fail a job, and you find out the next morning.

Automated Embedding addresses both with configurable quantization and built-in dynamic batching, with no manual tuning required.

For storage, configurable quantization gives you the right point on the accuracy/cost curve:

  • Scalar quantization (default) is roughly 4x smaller than float32, with retrieval accuracy nearly indistinguishable for most workloads.
  • Binary quantization is roughly 32x smaller, for workloads where the corpus is large enough that the recall trade-off pays for itself many times over.

For indexing, built-in dynamic batching automatically optimizes for the maximum tokens per request, adjusting batch size in real time based on document shape and size:

  • Automatic batch sizing adjusts in real time based on the actual shape and size of documents flowing through.
  • Built-in error recovery means a single malformed or oversized document doesn't take down a multi-million-document indexing job. The system isolates, retries, and continues.

Together, configurable quantization and dynamic batching mean agents can scale to hundreds of millions of documents without storage or indexing becoming a bottleneck.

Integrated feature engineering

Retrieval quality lives or dies on the quality of the input that gets embedded. Automated Embedding supports search on views, which means you can define a composite field declaratively, concatenating or transforming fields from the underlying collection. MongoDB Atlas automatically embeds and indexes the view's output, so feature engineering for retrieval becomes a query-language exercise instead of an ETL pipeline.

The simplest case is embedding a single field directly.

Figure 2. Enabling AI search on a single field in your document.

When retrieval requirements grow more complex, you can combine multiple fields into a single embedding source.

Figure 3. Enabling AI search on a combination of fields in your document.

For teams chasing the last 10-15% of retrieval accuracy, this is the lever that makes the difference. For everyone else, it's the reason you don't have to maintain a separate "search index document" alongside your operational schema.

Why this matters

The teams winning at agent applications treat search as a primitive, not an integration project. Automated Embedding provides retrieval that stays current as data changes, fast enough for agent response times, observable down to the token, affordable at any corpus size, and compliant out of the box.

Together, these qualities deliver a memory layer agents can depend on, built into the same platform where their data already lives.

Start building

Automated Embedding is now available in Public Preview on MongoDB Atlas across our supported regions. To get started:

  1. Spin up or select an Atlas cluster.
  2. Define an Automated Embedding index on your collection or view, pick a model, and you're done.
  3. Query with natural-language text - no client-side embedding required.

title: Why Actionable Banking Is the Critical Stepping Stone to Full Autonomy
summary:
Almost nothing is as important to someone today as their financial health. Most of us want to stay on top of what's happening with our bank accounts, like when a deposit clears so we can pay bills, if we're reaching our credit card limit, or if we have finally paid off that 30-year mortgage and can free up funds for that dream vacation or paying for our kid's college tuition. But we don't always get immediate feedback when transactions happen. That information often sits on the backend within our banks, and then days or weeks later we may get an email or alert with advice on investing or creating a payment plan.

But with actionable banking, this all becomes immediate. With the help of agentic AI, banks’ customers can quickly have a better understanding of steps they can take to make an investment or curb their spending with AI-powered insights. And people have said they want this.

In fact, in a survey conducted by Personetics of 2,000 bank customers(1), 70% said they strongly want their bank to proactively analyze their financial situation and 84% said they would likely switch to a bank that offers timely, relevant advice.

Actionable banking is also the safest first step toward autonomous banking. The agents act on events, but a human still makes the decision. MongoDB Atlas makes this possible by turning banking events into real-time triggers, unifying customer context in one platform, and keeping an auditable record of every agent action.

A three-step ladder: From passive to autonomous banking

Actionable banking serves as the bridge between legacy banking and fully autonomous finance:

Figure 1. The three-step ladder from passive to autonomous banking.

  • Passive banking: The customer initiates the interaction, most likely in response to a marketing campaign.
  • Actionable banking: The bank takes a proactive approach based on real-time event analysis. Agents act on events, but the customer still makes the decision.
  • Autonomous banking: A personal finance agent acts on its own, within limits the customer has set in advance and can revoke at any time.

The gap between actionable and autonomous is not the model. It is evidence: A bank can only grant agents a mandate once it can show what each agent saw, decided, and did, and who authorized it. Actionable banking is how that evidence gets logged into the corresponding audit trail.

Actionable banking also imposes a behavioral change. A dedicated agent will be continuously monitoring personal banking information, so its success will depend heavily on the guardrails implemented by the bank, in line with the customer's consent. More importantly, it should comply with data protection and AI regulations. Policymakers are moving fast to propose frameworks that incentivize innovation with the right controls in place. In the end, actionable banking's goal is to recommend the "best course of action" based on specific triggered events, but the customer is the one who decides and has the final word, which safeguards trust.

Below are three actionable agentic workflows and a reference architecture built on MongoDB Atlas and Atlas Agent Engine.

Three banking events, three agentic workflows

Every workflow starts with the Personal Finance Agent, which listens to daily banking activity through event-driven notifications. When a significant event arrives—a large deposit, an overdue card balance, a new mortgage—the agent opens an agentic workflow, hands the work to specialist agents, and returns a proposal the customer can discuss.

Figure 2. Actionable agentic workflow for proactive investments.

Proactive investment. A large deposit is the clearest signal of idle money. McKinsey estimates(2) that $23 trillion of the $170 trillion in consumer deposits worldwide sits in accounts paying zero or close to zero interest. The risk profile is not a formality; the EU requires the MiFID II suitability assessment before investment advice. So a risk assessment agent's output must be stored as evidence, not just passed along in a prompt. While the personal finance agent is responsible for the interaction and agreement with the customer, the wealth advisory agent is specialized in private banking, bringing the right proposal to the customer.

Figure 3. Actionable agentic workflow for proactive lending.

Proactive lending. An overdue card balance is both a credit risk and a moment of customer stress. Moving the balance to a cheaper installment loan costs the bank card margin, but keeps the customer and lowers its credit risk. Creditworthiness assessment of individuals is a high-risk use under the EU AI Act, so this workflow needs the strictest human oversight of the three. A credit risk officer needs to review, approve, and have all the arguments at hand for situations where customers and regulators would demand an explanation. A single agent with lending expertise can handle both risk assessment and advisory.

Figure 4. Actionable agentic workflow for proactive added-value services.

Proactive added-value services. A new mortgage changes the terms of what the customer needs to protect. The insurance agent reads the mortgage conditions and proposes an insurance policy with the proper coverage, as an optional offer and never as a condition of the loan.

Each workflow ends in "push and discuss," not "execute." That is what makes it actionable rather than autonomous.

Actionable banking reference architecture on MongoDB

Figure 5. Actionable banking reference architecture.

Systems of record write into MongoDB Atlas, which holds the operational view of each customer. Change streams turn business moments into events for the personal finance agent. Specialist agents run on Atlas Agent Engine, sharing customer context through a common memory layer with per-agent access controls. Every agent action and tool call is recorded in a single, immutable audit trail. The customer's decision flows back as memory for the next interaction and as evidence for the regulator.

The business case for actionable banking

McKinsey(3) estimates that banks that fail to adapt to agentic AI could see global profit pools fall by about $170 billion, or roughly 9%, as customers' own agents start moving idle money. Actionable banking is both the defense and the offense: The bank's agent makes the better offer before someone else's agent does.

Why banking agent projects stall and what the platform must fix

Banks are not short of agent pilots; they are short of agents in production. Gartner(4) expects over 40% of agentic AI projects to be canceled by the end of 2027 over cost, unclear value, or weak risk controls. Actionable banking runs into three engineering problems behind those numbers.

Atlas Agent Engine(5), in public preview since September of 2026, unifies runtime, memory, and governance in one layer, with sandboxed execution and agent identity built in. It is neutral across models and frameworks and built on open standards such as MCP and A2A, so a personal finance agent can delegate to specialist agents without tying the bank to one vendor's model or cloud. Paysafe is already exploring an agent engine-based agent so its analysts stop stitching together data from multiple systems by hand when investigating unusual payment activity.

A change in behavior, not only in technology

Actionable banking is largely an engineering pattern. Autonomous banking also requires a shift in trust and behavior. Customers must delegate, banks must accept accountability for agents that act, and regulators must be satisfied that both are safe.

The relationship manager becomes an agent. The attention of a private banker, someone who notices the bonus, the new mortgage, and the missed payment, has always been rationed by cost. A personal agent makes it available to every customer, around the clock, with memory of every conversation. Banks that get this right keep the relationship with the customer. Those that don’t may end up as the infrastructure for another party’s agent.

Trust is the ultimate mandate. The most critical challenge is not technical. Delegating decision-making authority to an agent—and granting it permission to act on behalf of an organization or an individual—turns machines into active economic participants. That is a disruptive behavioral change for customers, regulators, and banks alike. Banks have always sold trust; in autonomous banking, they must also prove it, action by action and mandate by mandate.

Start simply with one event, one workflow, or one governed proposal. That is the first step toward autonomous banking, and the data platform underneath decides how far you can take it.

title: Building an Agentic Warehouse Management System—Part 3: Tools, Decisions, and Actions
summary:
If you haven’t read the first two parts yet, I recommend starting with Part 1: Where AI Agents Add Value and Part 2: Designing and Planning the Agent. There, we introduced the WMS scenario, discussed where an AI agent can add value, and built the first stages of the implementation with Java and Spring AI.

In this third and final part, we will build on the execution plan created in Part 2 and focus on the remaining stages of the agent workflow. We will see how each task is executed using controlled tools, how operational and business context is gathered, how the replenishment decision is made, and how the agent acts on that decision when necessary.

From plan to execution

Let’s revisit the complete agent flow. The first stages: Define the Agent, Trigger the Agent, and Plan, were covered in the previous article. Now we will focus on executing the tasks, using the available tools, gathering context, and making the replenishment decision.

Figure 1. Agent Lifecycle: Execute, Decide, and Complete.

Execute tasks with controlled tools

With the execution plan created in Part 2, the AgentRunner starts processing the tasks one at a time. For each task, the runner reads its description and capability, executes it, stores the result, and then continues with the next task:

Before executing a task, the runner selects only the tools associated with its capability:

When the task is executed, the executor receives the current goal, the results produced by previous tasks, the current task, and only the tools available for its capability:

The result of each completed task becomes part of the context available to the tasks that follow. This allows the agent to progressively gather the information it needs before making the replenishment decision.

At the same time, the capability assigned to each task defines which tools are available during its execution. This preserves the boundaries we established earlier: an ANALYSIS task, for example, can inspect information from the WMS, but it does not have access to tools that create a replenishment request.

Figure 2. Agent running.

Accessing operational data

During ANALYSIS tasks, the agent can use controlled tools to retrieve operational data from the WMS, such as inventory, invoice movements, stock movements, and pending replenishments.

For example, one of the available tools retrieves the stock movements generated by an outbound invoice:

With Spring AI, methods like this can be exposed to the model using annotations such as @Tool and @ToolParam. The executor can then call them when the current task requires that information.

The complete application exposes additional tools for retrieving inventory, invoice movements, pending replenishments, and other operational data. We will not cover each one here, but they follow the same idea.

Retrieving depositor policies

The depositor policies are also accessed through a dedicated tool exposed by the POLICY capability. In our application, each depositor can register business rules through the Depositor Policies page. For example, a policy may define a seven-day lead time or require at least 500 units per replenishment request:

Figure 3. Depositor policies screen.

These policies are stored as natural-language documents, which allows us to retrieve them using semantic search instead of relying solely on exact keywords. For example:

title: Introducing Atlas App Connections: Secure, One-Click Access for AI Tools
summary:
For builders using AI coding tools, speed is everything. Integrations that require generating a credential, filing an access request, or waiting on a custom build can stop momentum (and productivity) in its tracks.

Until now, connecting an external application like an AI coding assistant to a MongoDB Atlas account introduced some of that friction. The only way to do so was by sharing long-lived service account credentials, a workaround that slowed builders down and left administrators managing a security risk they were reluctant to accept. Faced with that tradeoff, some organizations avoided third-party integrations, or defaulted to whatever tool was already the default in their AI stack, whether or not it was the best fit.

MongoDB Atlas App Connections closes that gap. It enables builders to securely connect AI coding tools to their MongoDB Atlas account with a single click. Built on OAuth 2.1, an industry-standard authorization framework, App Connections allows AI clients to act on the user's behalf via the MongoDB Atlas MCP Server, without long-lived credentials to generate, share, or manage.

Available now in Atlas App Connections

With Atlas App Connections, builders can connect their AI coding tools to MongoDB Atlas through the Atlas MCP Server, including:

  • ChatGPT

  • Claude

  • Claude Code

  • Codex CLI

  • Cursor

  • Devin

  • Devin Desktop

  • Grok

  • Grok CLI

Once connected, these tools can provision, manage, and query MongoDB Atlas resources directly on the builder's behalf, whether that means spinning up a new cluster, checking on an existing one, or working with the data inside it, based on the access the connecting user already has. Administrators control how far that access extends, choosing between read-only and full access before any AI client can act.

Using App Connections in practice

Here's what that looks like for a builder, using Claude as an example. Assuming Claude is already running, connecting a MongoDB Atlas account takes three steps:

  1. Install the MongoDB plugin by running /plugin install mongodb-atlas@claude-plugins-official.

  2. Grant Claude access by running /mcp, selecting plugin:mongodb-atlas:mongodb-atlas, and choosing Authenticate.

  3. Approve the one-click authorization.

Installing the plugin also adds a set of skills that teach Claude how to work with MongoDB Atlas, and installs MongoDB's remote MCP server behind the scenes. From there, the developer can simply ask Claude to provision a new database cluster, and Claude does it: translating that request into secure Atlas API calls through the Atlas MCP Server. There's no credential to generate or share to make that happen. The administrator overseeing that Atlas organization still has full visibility into the connection and can revoke it at any time.

What you get if you’re building

For builders, speed and security have always felt like a tradeoff. Bottlenecked by integration setup friction, many resorted to workarounds such as sharing high-risk, long-lived credentials just to keep building.

Atlas App Connections removes that tradeoff. A single click securely authorizes AI coding tools to connect to Atlas. There are no credentials to share and no manual configuration to manage. Builders stay in their flow, building at the speed of AI, without ever compromising account security to get there.

What you get if you’re governing an organization

For administrators, the calculus has been just as fraught. Engineering teams need modern AI coding tools to stay competitive, but granting those tools access via opaque, shared service accounts can mean losing track of who or what is actually acting on an organization's data.

Atlas App Connections eliminates that challenge. Access to connect AI clients to Atlas is disabled by default in existing organizations, and administrators must opt in. New organizations created during sign-up start with that access enabled, so first-time users get the best possible AI experience from the outset. Once approved, every action is attributed to both the application and the person who authorized it, visible in Atlas activity feeds. Administrators decide exactly how long an AI client's access can last before it requires re-approval, and can turn off AI client access for the entire organization at any time. Individual users can revoke their own connections whenever they choose. Atlas App Connections helps eliminate shadow AI without standing in the way of engineering teams doing their jobs.

How Atlas App Connections works

Connecting an AI coding tool to Atlas using App Connections takes five steps:

  1. The user installs MongoDB's plugin or connector for their AI client.

  2. The user requests to connect their MongoDB Atlas account from within that client.

  3. The client redirects the user to Atlas.

  4. The user logs in and sees a consent screen naming the application and exactly what it's asking to access.

  5. All the user has to do is click “Approve” and the application is enabled to act on their behalf through the Atlas MCP Server.

Behind the scenes, that approval gives the AI coding tool permission to obtain a short-lived access token and a refresh token on the user's behalf, so it doesn't need to ask the user to log in again for every action. The tool uses that access to provision, manage, and query Atlas resources through the Atlas MCP Server, scoped to whatever access the connecting user already has. All of this happens automatically, invisible to both the user and the application.

A few properties of that access are worth knowing:

  • User-scoped: The AI client can only take actions for which the user has permissions. If a user's Atlas permissions change, the AI client's access automatically changes with them.

  • Revocable: Users can revoke an AI client's access at any time, and it takes effect within 15 minutes.

  • Auditable: Every delegated action is attributed to both the AI client and the user it acted on behalf of.

  • Governed by the organization: Delegated access to AI clients is disabled by default. Atlas organization owners decide whether to turn it on, and for AI clients specifically, whether to allow read-only or full access. If an owner turns off delegation for the entire organization, that change takes effect immediately.
